# Craft — Picked green, extracted cold | Makaron

URL: https://makaron.com/craft/

## Picked green Extracted cold

Discover Our craft ↓

Grown, early harvested, cold extracted and tinned — all in one place.

Minimum intervention, maximum of what the fruit carried off the tree.

### We pick olives while still green, when their polyphenols are at their peak.

Early fruit yields less oil — roughly a litre from twelve to fifteen kilos — but far more of what matters. Baskets reach the mill the same day, before the fruit can warm or bruise.

### Cold extraction below 27°C, so aroma and nutrients survive the mill.

A Neo-Classic system presses the fruit without warming it or adding water. Heat strips a green oil of its character, and water washes out its polyphenols; keeping both out of the process is what leaves the aroma and the peppery finish intact.

### Every lot is lab-tested before it fills a tin.

Acidity, peroxide and total phenols are measured for each pressing. The lot number on your tin matches the certificate, so the oil you pour is the oil we tested.

### Real oil, real taste

One pressing, in the size you cook at. Light-proof tin keeps the polyphenols where they belong.

Gift set £119.99 2.5 L tin + refillable bottle

# At the table — How to use early-harvest olive oil | Makaron

URL: https://makaron.com/at-the-table/

## A green oil wants tasting

Explore In the kitchen ↓

Use it where you will taste it.

Raw over food is where the peppery finish and the polyphenols show.

“The peppery catch at the back of the throat is the point, not a flaw.”

On tasting early-harvest oil

### At the table

One oil that carries a whole kitchen — from the first spoonful at breakfast to the last thread off the heat.

- 01 Raw & finishing — over tomatoes, white cheese and warm bread, or across grilled fish.

- 02 Salads — whisk with lemon and salt; the peppery finish does the rest.

- 03 Cooking — stable for everyday heat; add the last spoonful off the flame.

- 04 Storage — keep cool and dark; decant a smaller bottle for the counter.

# The grove — Edremit Gulf, Türkiye | Makaron

URL: https://makaron.com/grove/

## Why we keep it small

Discover The grove ↓

We choose accuracy over speed,

quality over quantity,

and one traceable grove over a lesser blend.

Grown in the right place, pressed at the right time, bottled with as little between tree and tin as we can manage.

### The grove

Our grove covers a hundred and twenty acres on the slopes between the Kozak mountains and the Edremit Gulf, and every tree on it is of the Edremit variety. Olives have been pressed on this land since 1864. The youngest of our trees are at least thirty years old, and we never bring in fruit from other sources.

### FAQ

Early harvest

Olives picked while still green, before they ripen and darken. Green fruit holds the most polyphenols and gives an oil with more aroma, a livelier peppery finish and lower acidity — at the cost of a lower yield.

Polyphenols

They are the antioxidants behind the peppery catch at the back of your throat. Anything above 350 mg/kg is considered high; this lot measures 452 mg/kg.

Storage and shelf life

Cool, dark and sealed. Light is olive oil's enemy, which is why we fill light-proof tin rather than clear glass. Use within a year of opening.

Trade and wholesale

Yes. The catering case holds six 2.5 L tins, with the same lot and certificate as every retail tin. Use the trade enquiry on the contact page for standing orders.

# How to read an olive oil label — and the one word that predicts quality | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/how-to-read-an-olive-oil-label/
Published: 2026-10-12

[Buying](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## How to read an olive oil label — and the one word that predicts quality

Makaron — 12 Oct 2026

Takeaways

- “Extra virgin” is a floor, not a grade of excellence.

- Harvest date beats a best-before date.

- Acidity and polyphenol figures are the real signal.

### Start with the harvest, not the marketing

Most bottles lead with words that feel reassuring and mean very little on their own. “Natural,” “cold pressed,” even “extra virgin” describe a minimum standard, not the character of what is inside. The information that actually predicts how an oil tastes, and how good it is for you, is usually printed small, or not at all.

The single most useful thing to look for is a harvest date. Olive oil does not improve with age; it fades. An oil pressed from this season's fruit and stored away from light is worth more than one with a distant best-before date and no harvest date at all.

### The two numbers that matter

If the producer prints them, free acidity and total polyphenols tell you most of the story. Free acidity below 0.8% is the legal ceiling for extra virgin; a genuinely early, carefully milled oil sits far lower. Polyphenols — the antioxidants responsible for the peppery finish — fade as fruit ripens, so a high figure is a sign the olives were picked green and pressed fast.

If a producer will print the numbers, they have usually earned the right to.

Makaron

### Origin, in one place

Look for a single named origin — a region, ideally a grove — rather than “product of EU” or a list of countries. Blends assembled from several sources are not necessarily bad, but they cannot tell you when or how the fruit was picked, and the best lots are rarely sold that way.

A reputable producer can back their figures with a certificate of analysis tied to the lot number on the tin. That traceability — one grove, one pressing, one tested lot — is the difference between a label that reassures and a label that proves.

---

# Polyphenols, explained in a paragraph | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/polyphenols-explained/
Published: 2026-09-28

[Buying](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## Polyphenols, explained in a paragraph

Makaron — 28 Sep 2026

Takeaways

- They are the compounds behind the green intensity and the peppery finish.

- Green fruit carries the most; ripening, heat, light and time take them away.

- The cough at the back of the throat is a feature, not a fault.

### The paragraph

Polyphenols are a family of natural antioxidants the olive tree makes to protect its fruit. In the oil they show up as a green grip on the tongue and a peppery catch at the back of the throat — oleocanthal, oleacein, oleuropein and hydroxytyrosol are the ones most often measured. They are at their highest in green, unripe fruit and fall steadily as the olive darkens, and again with every day the oil spends warm, bright or open. An oil with a strong, clean peppery finish is therefore an oil that was picked early, milled quickly and kept well. That is the whole idea.

### Why we chase them

Everything else about our method follows from that paragraph. We pick while the fruit is still green, because that is when the polyphenols peak. We accept the lower yield that comes with it. We press below 27°C, because heat strips them out. We put the oil in tin, because light does the same. None of this is a style choice; it is simply what keeps the compounds in the oil long enough to reach your kitchen.

The green edge and the peppery finish are not defects to be softened. They are the evidence.

Makaron

### What the numbers mean

Total polyphenols are reported in milligrams per kilogram. Many supermarket oils fall well under 200 mg/kg by the time they are sold; the European health claim for olive oil polyphenols requires at least 5 mg of hydroxytyrosol and its derivatives per 20 g of oil, which works out at 250 mg/kg. Early-harvest oils from healthy groves can sit comfortably above that. Every Makaron lot is tested, and the figure travels with the lot number on the tin.

### How to taste for them

Warm a small glass of oil in your hands, cover it, then uncover and smell: grass, artichoke, tomato leaf. Take a little into your mouth with air, as you would a wine. A green, grassy grip arrives first, on the tongue. Then the peppery catch — and, with a young, high-phenol oil, a cough. Nobody has ever been sorry about the cough.

---

# Why we sell oil in tin, not glass | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/why-tin-not-glass/
Published: 2026-09-14

[Storage](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## Why we sell oil in tin, not glass

Makaron — 14 Sep 2026

Takeaways

- Light and oxygen are what age an oil, and tin shuts both out completely.

- Tin is lighter, travels without breaking and keeps the oil cooler.

- Decant a little at a time into a dark bottle for the table.

### The enemies are light, air and heat

Olive oil is a fresh product. It does not spoil the way milk does, but it declines — the aromas flatten, the peppery finish softens, and eventually it turns flat and waxy. Three things drive that decline: light, which breaks down the chlorophyll and the polyphenols; oxygen, which oxidises the fats; and heat, which accelerates both. A clear glass bottle on a shelf under shop lighting is the worst place an oil can be.

### What tin does

A tin is opaque. Not tinted, not dark — opaque. No light reaches the oil from the moment it is filled until the moment you pour it. The walls are thin, so the oil does not hold heat the way a thick bottle does, and the tin itself is light enough that a 2.5 litre size is practical to ship and to lift. It will not break in the post, and it does not need the bubble wrap that glass does.

Glass is for showing an oil. Tin is for keeping one.

Makaron

### Keeping it at home

Store the tin in a cupboard, away from the hob and the oven. Close it after each use. An opened tin will keep its character for several months; a sealed one, kept cool, considerably longer. If you buy the larger size, decant a week or two's worth into a smaller dark bottle for the table and leave the rest sealed — which is exactly why our gift set pairs a 2.5 litre tin with a refillable bottle.

One last thing: do not refrigerate it. The cold makes the oil cloud and thicken, and the condensation that forms each time it is taken out does more harm than the cupboard ever would.

---

# Inside the 2026 pressing, week by week | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/inside-the-2026-pressing/
Published: 2026-10-28

[Harvest](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## Inside the 2026 pressing, week by week

Makaron — 28 Oct 2026

Takeaways

- Picking started on the lower slopes in the first days of October.

- Every crate is milled the day it is picked.

- The first tins were filled before the month was out.

### Week one — the lower slopes

The harvest opened in the first week of October, on the lower terraces nearest the gulf where the fruit ripens earliest. The olives were still firmly green, a few just beginning to turn at the shoulder, which is exactly the point we want them. Nets down in the morning, fruit stripped by hand and with small rakes, crates loaded by early afternoon and at the mill before the heat of the day had gone out of them. Nothing stays overnight.

### Week two — first oil

The first lot came off the press mid-month. Leaves blown off, fruit washed, crushed, and the paste worked gently and cold — never above 27°C — before the oil is separated. The first taste is always the same shock: electric green, artichoke and cut grass on the nose, a green grip on the tongue, and a peppery catch that makes everyone in the mill cough. A sample from the lot went to the laboratory the same day.

The best oil of the year is usually the one that made the mill cough hardest.

Makaron

### Week three — up the hill

Picking moved to the higher ground beneath the Kozak mountains, where the nights are cooler and the fruit ripens a week or two behind. The oil from these trees is leaner and more peppery than the first lot; blended within the same pressing, the two balance each other. The early lots settled in the steel tanks, in the dark, with the fine sediment dropping out of their own accord.

### Week four — into tin

With the laboratory results back and within our own limits, the first lot was racked off its sediment and the filling line started. Each tin carries the lot number of the pressing it came from, so the certificate you can read online is the certificate for the oil in your hand. The 2026 oil is available now; the higher-ground lots will follow as they settle.

# Acidity, and what the number really tells you | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/olive-oil-acidity-explained/
Published: 2026-08-18

[Buying](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## Acidity, and what the number really tells you

Makaron — 18 Aug 2026

Takeaways

- “Acidity” is free fatty acid content, not sourness — you cannot taste it.

- It rises when fruit is bruised, fermented or left waiting before milling.

- Under 0.8% is the extra virgin standard; it is one test among several.

### Not what it sounds like

The word misleads almost everyone. Free acidity has nothing to do with how sour or sharp an oil tastes; you cannot detect it on the palate at all. It is a laboratory measure of free fatty acids — mostly oleic acid — expressed as a percentage. Fatty acids are “free” when they have broken loose from the triglyceride molecules that make up the oil, and that happens when the fruit is damaged.

### What raises it

Olives that have been bruised in picking, attacked by fly, left in heaps to warm and ferment, or simply kept waiting for days before milling all arrive at the press with more free fatty acids. So do olives picked from the ground. Acidity is, in effect, a record of how the fruit was treated between the tree and the mill. That is why it is used as the first line of the extra virgin standard: an oil must be below 0.8% to carry the name at all.

Acidity does not describe the taste of an oil. It describes the care taken with the fruit before pressing.

Makaron

### What it cannot tell you

A low figure proves the fruit was sound and handled quickly; it does not, on its own, tell you the oil is aromatic, or that it is rich in polyphenols, or that it has been stored well since. For that there are other tests — peroxide value and ultraviolet absorbance for oxidation, total polyphenols for the antioxidants, and a trained tasting panel for defects and fruitiness. We run the laboratory tests on every lot and keep the results with the lot number, because one good number is a claim; the full sheet is a record.

---

# Early vs late harvest: a tasting | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/early-vs-late-harvest-tasting/
Published: 2026-08-04

[Harvest](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## Early vs late harvest: a tasting

Makaron — 4 Aug 2026

Takeaways

- Early oil is green, bright and peppery; late oil is soft, ripe and buttery.

- Early picking gives far less oil per kilo of fruit — and far more character.

- Both have their uses. We only make one of them.

### Two oils from the same trees

Pick an Edremit olive in early October, while it is green and hard, and press it that day, and you get one oil. Leave the same fruit on the tree until December, when it is black, soft and heavy with oil, and you get another. Same grove, same variety, same mill. Tasted side by side the difference is startling, and it explains most of what people argue about when they argue about olive oil.

### The early oil

Bright green in the glass. On the nose: cut grass, artichoke, tomato leaf, green almond. In the mouth it is green and brisk first, then builds to a peppery catch at the throat that lingers. The texture is lean, almost brisk. This is an oil for finishing — over grilled fish, a plate of white beans, bread, tomatoes, soup — where that intensity is the point. The polyphenol content is at its peak, and so is the price of making it: twelve to fifteen kilos of green fruit for a single litre.

### The late oil

Pale gold, sometimes with a straw tint. Softer and rounder on the nose — ripe fruit, a little banana, nuts. The green edge has largely gone and the peppery finish is a murmur. It is pleasant, forgiving and good for cooking in volume, and the trees give two or three times as much of it. Its polyphenols are a fraction of the early oil's, and it will not keep as long.

Late oil is easy to like. Early oil is worth the trouble of understanding.

Makaron

### Why we pick early

There is nothing wrong with a ripe oil. But the character of this grove — the sea air, the hill behind it, the age of the trees — shows in the green oil and is smoothed away in the late one. We take the lower yield and press only early-harvest fruit, because that is the oil that tastes of where it came from.

---

# The Edremit olive, and why it suits this coast | Makaron Journal

URL: https://makaron.com/journal/the-edremit-olive/
Published: 2026-07-20

[Harvest](https://makaron.com/journal/)

## The Edremit olive, and why it suits this coast

Makaron — 20 Jul 2026

Takeaways

- Edremit — also called Ayvalık — is the native olive of Turkey’s north Aegean coast.

- A small, oil-rich fruit that gives a fruity, balanced, gently peppery oil.

- The gulf, the mountains and the old trees do the rest.

### One variety, one coast

Along the shore of the Edremit Gulf — Ayvalık, Burhaniye, Edremit — nearly every grove is planted with the same olive. It goes by the name of the bay, or of the town, and it has been grown here for as long as anyone has kept records. The fruit is small to medium, oval, and unusually rich in oil for its size, which is why the region has always been an oil coast rather than a table-olive one.

### What it tastes like

Pressed early, Edremit gives an oil that is fruity and green rather than fierce: artichoke and fresh-cut grass, a clean green edge, a peppery finish that is present without being aggressive, and a notable sweetness underneath. It is an oil of balance. Where some varieties shout, this one carries — it makes a plain plate of beans taste finished and does not overwhelm a piece of fish.

The tree chose this coast long before we did. We only had to keep it.

Makaron

### Why here

The grove sits on the slopes between the Kozak mountains and the sea. The mountains hold off the worst of the northern winter; the gulf keeps the summers from scorching; the breeze off the water dries the leaves and keeps the fruit healthy; and the thin, stony, lime-rich soil makes the trees work for their water, which concentrates the fruit. Our youngest trees are at least thirty years old. Many are far older, and old trees, deep-rooted and slow, give the most consistent fruit of all.

The farm has pressed Edremit olives on this ground since 1864. No fruit comes in from other sources. What is in the tin is this variety, this slope, this season — which is as much as any olive oil can honestly claim.

# Privacy policy | Makaron

URL: https://makaron.com/privacy/

[Makaron](https://makaron.com/)

## Privacy policy

Last updated 31 October 2026

### 1. Who is responsible for your data

Metrics34 UK Limited of 81 Turners Hill, Cheshunt, Waltham Cross, Hertfordshire, EN8 9BD is the data controller for the personal data collected through this website. Questions about this policy can be sent to [hello@makaron.com](mailto:hello@makaron.com).

### 2. What we collect

- Order information — your name, address, email address, telephone number and the items you buy. Payment card details are handled by our payment provider and are not stored by us.

- Correspondence — anything you send us by email or through the contact form.

- Harvest list — your email address if you subscribe to our updates.

- Technical data — IP address, browser type and pages visited, collected through server logs and any analytics tools described in section 6.

### 3. How we use it, and on what basis

- To fulfil your order, process payment and handle returns — necessary to perform our contract with you.

- To answer your enquiries — our legitimate interest in responding to people who contact us.

- To send harvest updates and offers — with your consent, which you can withdraw at any time using the link in any email.

- To keep accounting and tax records — a legal obligation.

- To secure and improve the website — our legitimate interest in running it properly.

### 4. Who we share it with

We share personal data only with the suppliers who help us run the business: our payment provider, the platform that hosts this website and sends our emails, and our accountants. Each is bound by contract to use the data only for the service they provide to us. We do not sell personal data.

Where a supplier is based outside the United Kingdom, we rely on safeguards recognised under UK data protection law, such as an adequacy decision or the International Data Transfer Agreement.

### 5. How long we keep it

Order records are kept for six years after the end of the financial year in which the order was placed, as required for tax purposes. Harvest list subscriptions are kept until you unsubscribe. Correspondence is kept for [two years] after our last exchange. Technical logs are kept for [90 days].

### 6. Cookies

Cookies are small files stored on your device. This website uses three kinds:

- Strictly necessary — needed for the site to work: the basket, the checkout, security, and remembering your cookie choice. These are always on and do not require consent.

- Analytics — anonymous statistics about how the site is used (pages visited, time on page, device type), so that we can improve it. Set only with your consent.

- Advertising — cookies placed by advertising partners to show relevant adverts and measure campaigns. Set only with your consent.

When you first visit, a banner asks which cookies you accept; nothing non-essential is set until you choose. You can change or withdraw your choice at any time using “Cookie settings” in the footer, or by clearing cookies in your browser. Where consent is given, it is recorded with the date and time and kept for twelve months, after which we ask again.

### 7. Your rights

Under UK data protection law you have the right to ask for a copy of the personal data we hold about you, to have inaccurate data corrected, to have your data erased where we no longer need it, to object to or restrict certain processing, and to receive data you have given us in a portable form. To exercise any of these rights, email [hello@makaron.com](mailto:hello@makaron.com). We will respond within one month.

If you are unhappy with how we have handled your data, you can complain to the Information Commissioner's Office at ico.org.uk.

### 8. Changes to this policy

We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top shows when it was last changed.
